📌 Tehran, IRNA – The Islamic Resistance in Iraq has rejected Saudi Arabia’s claim that drone attacks against oil facilities in the kingdom originated from Iraqi territory, warning Riyadh against any “foolish action” based on the allegation.

According to Iraqi media reports, the group said in a statement on Monday that any such action by Saudi Arabia would be met with a severe response that would leave the kingdom “deeply regretful.”
​
The statement said Riyadh’s repeated accusations that Iraq was the origin of attacks on oil facilities in the country’s Eastern Province and the capital, Riyadh, reflected continued hostility toward Iraq.
​
It dismissed the allegations as an attempt to justify Saudi Arabia’s inability to respond to attacks launched from Yemen and to cover up its “failures and crimes.”
​
Reaffirming its rejection of speculation and accusations against Iraq, the Islamic Resistance in Iraq said the Saudi government should lift the blockade on Yemen instead of accusing the Yemeni people in an effort to justify its own failures.
​
Earlier, the Saudi Ministry of Defense claimed that oil facilities in two areas of the kingdom’s Eastern Province and in Riyadh had been targeted in drone attacks launched from inside Iraq.
​
Following the claim, Iraqi Prime Minister and Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces Ali Falih al-Zaidi instructed the country’s security authorities on Monday to investigate the Saudi Defense Ministry’s statement regarding the alleged drone attacks from Iraqi territory.
​
In a statement, military spokesman Sabah al-Numan said the Iraqi government remained firmly committed to the principles of good neighborliness and would not allow Iraqi territory to be used as a transit route or launching point for aggression against brotherly or friendly countries.
​
Al-Numan said the government was reviewing available evidence and information and would take legal action against anyone found to have been involved based on the outcome of the investigation.
​
The Saudi allegation came after authorities in Sana’a had announced that the Yemeni Armed Forces had targeted sensitive sites inside Saudi Arabia in response to Saudi attacks.
​
The Yemeni Armed Forces have said they will continue their operations until the 12-year blockade on Yemen is lifted.

How social media is being banned around the world

Just a couple of years ago, only one country wanted to ban social media for children. Now it's 25.

Australia has banned social media for anyone under 16. The UK is introducing its ban starting in 2027, with France, Spain, and Turkey following.

The justification is the same everywhere: protecting children. It's also a message that tends to resonate with the public, making these laws much easier to pass.

Infinite scroll, autoplay, push notifications — all of these are now increasingly being treated as addictive design features. In other words, social media is starting to be regulated much like cigarettes or gambling.

The problem is, bans by themselves don't actually work.

The only way to reliably keep kids off these platforms is to verify everyone's age — using government ID, banking information, or biometrics.

In other words, if governments want to keep teenagers off apps like TikTok, they also have to eliminate anonymity for adults. That's exactly what many of these countries are now discussing. The UK has already started putting this into practice.

So the global trend looks like this: phase out online anonymity under the banner of protecting children. Want to use the internet? Be prepared to submit your personal information and verify your identity.

Teach your kids at home.
